\begin{proof}
We prove that infinitely many primes are congruent to $3$ modulo $4$. Suppose, for contradiction, that the complete list of such primes is $p_1=3,p_2,\ldots,p_n$. Let
\[
 a=4p_2\cdots p_n+3.
\]
Then $a\equiv3\pmod4$. Since $a$ is odd, all its prime divisors are odd. If every prime divisor of $a$ were congruent to $1$ modulo $4$, then $a$, being their product with multiplicity, would be congruent to $1$ modulo $4$, a contradiction. Hence some prime divisor $q$ of $a$ satisfies $q\equiv3\pmod4$.

For $i\ge2$, we have $a\equiv3\pmod{p_i}$, so $p_i\nmid a$ because $p_i\ne3$. Also,
\[
 a\equiv p_2\cdots p_n\not\equiv0\pmod3,
\]
so $3=p_1\nmid a$. Thus $q$ is a prime congruent to $3$ modulo $4$ not among $p_1,\ldots,p_n$, contradicting completeness. Therefore infinitely many primes are congruent to $-1$ modulo $4$.
\end{proof}

\[

Then $N\equiv3\pmod4$ and $N$ is odd. Factor $N$ into primes. At least one prime divisor $q$ of $N$ must be $3$ modulo $4$: otherwise every prime divisor would be $1$ modulo $4$, forcing $N\equiv1\pmod4$.

For each $i\ge2$, $N\equiv3\pmod{p_i}$, so $p_i$ does not divide $N$. Moreover,
\[
N\equiv p_2\cdots p_n\equiv1\cdot\ldots\cdot1\equiv1\pmod3,
\]
so $p_1=3$ does not divide $N$. Consequently, $q$ is a prime congruent to $3$ modulo $4$ that is absent from the supposed complete list, a contradiction. Hence there are infinitely many primes congruent to $-1$ modulo $4$.
\end{proof}

\[

\]

We now verify that $q$ is not on the list. If $i\ge2$, then
\[
N\equiv3\pmod{p_i},
\]
so $p_i\nmid N$, since $p_i\ne3$. Also, modulo $3$,
\[
N\equiv p_2\cdots p_n\not\equiv0\pmod3,
\]
because none of the distinct primes $p_2,\ldots,p_n$ equals $3$. Hence $p_1=3\nmid N$. Therefore $q$ is a prime congruent to $3$, equivalently $-1$, modulo $4$ that is not in the complete list, a contradiction. Thus there are infinitely many primes congruent to $-1$ modulo $4$.
\end{proof}
